Clinical Vignette: Karim

Karim was forty-eight when the building collapsed. He had been in Beirut for a design consultation—a two-week trip to work with a luxury hotel chain on their lobby renovation. He remembered the morning light through the café window where he'd been reviewing fabric samples, the weight of the espresso cup in his hand, the particular warmth of the Lebanese sun on his neck. Then the sound, a sound he could not describe to anyone who hadn't heard it, followed by the sensation of falling, of being crushed, of breathing dust instead of air. He was pulled from the rubble after six hours. His left arm was fractured in two places. He came home to his apartment in Manhattan with a cast and a prescription for pain medication, telling himself he was lucky.

Three months later, Karim could not explain to his ex-wife why he had stopped coming to their son's soccer games. The truth was that the moment he stepped into the open field—the sky so exposed, the crowd so unpredictable—his body flooded with certainty that something terrible was about to happen. He would scan the bleachers for exits, trace the perimeter of the field in his mind, identify which fence he could climb if he needed to escape. By the time his son kicked the ball, Karim's chest was tight and his mind was somewhere else entirely. He stopped going. His son, now sixteen, had stopped asking him to come.

The triggers were unpredictable and everywhere. A sudden noise—a car backfiring, a dropped tray in a restaurant—and Karim's mind would fracture. The memory would come not as a coherent narrative but as disconnected pieces: the taste of concrete and blood, the sensation of heat against his skin, his hand reaching for something in the darkness. These fragments didn't fit together into a story he could understand or contain. They felt like they were happening now, in the present moment, even as he sat safely in his studio or on the subway. When the memory arrived, he couldn't think straight. His concentration evaporated. He would leave meetings abruptly, telling his assistant he had another appointment. He had lost two major clients in the past year because of his unreliability.

The nausea came with the memories. So did a hyperawareness of temperature—a sudden warmth on his skin could send him spiraling back to the dust and heat of the collapse. These triggers activated something in him that demanded action. He couldn't simply sit with the sensation. Instead, he threw himself into work, staying at the studio until midnight, redesigning the same collection five times over, keeping his hands and mind occupied so relentlessly that sleep became impossible. Busyness was a cage he had built to contain the panic, but it was a cage with bars that were slowly closing in.

When the vigilance took hold—and it took hold constantly now—Karim found himself checking the locks on his apartment door three, sometimes four times before bed. He would walk through his studio in the morning and check the emergency exits, the windows, the structural integrity of the walls. At restaurants, he always positioned himself with a view of the door. This constant scanning for danger, this exhausting surveillance of his environment, made it impossible to relax, and the inability to relax fed the memories. Without distraction, without movement, without the armor of busyness, the fragments would surface again. When they did, he would hurt himself—pressing the edge of his cast against his forearm until it left marks, or clenching his fists until his nails drew blood from his palms. The physical pain was a way of asserting control, of proving to himself that he could feel something other than the helplessness of that morning.

The cycle had tightened around him so completely that he barely recognized when he had stopped living and started only surviving. It was his sister who finally insisted he come in. She said he looked like he was disappearing. Karim knew she was right. What frightened him most now was not the memory itself, but the possibility that he might never feel safe again, that the building would never finish collapsing, that this fragmented, terrifying present was all he had left.
